faq.a: CTA provides excellent anatomic detail and is often sufficient for diagnosis, but catheter angiography is still needed for therapeutic interventions.
Use non‑contrast MRI/MRA, duplex ultrasound, or consider low‑dose contrast with pre‑hydration if renal function allows.
faq.q: What if iodinated contrast is contraindicated?

faq.a: Apply dose‑modulation, limit scan range, use iterative reconstruction, and avoid repeat scans when prior images are adequate.
faq.q: How to reduce radiation exposure in CTA?

exam: A 45‑year‑old man with sudden tearing back pain and hypotension—what imaging do you order and why? — CTA of the thoraco‑abdominal aorta; it rapidly confirms dissection and guides surgery.

You see a crescent‑shaped low‑attenuation area in the aortic wall on CTA—what is the diagnosis and next step? — Intramural hematoma; admit to ICU, control blood pressure, arrange urgent surgical consult.
A patient with renal failure needs evaluation for pulmonary embolism—what alternative to CTPA can you use? — Ventilation‑perfusion scan or bedside echocardiography; avoid iodinated contrast.

CTA shows a 7 mm carotid artery stenosis in an asymptomatic patient—how do you manage? — Medical therapy (antiplatelet, statin, BP control); consider endarterectomy only if symptomatic or >70 % stenosis.

During CTA you notice contrast extravasation in the abdomen—what does this indicate and what is your immediate action? — Active bleeding; call surgical team for possible embolisation or operative control.

Explain why timing of contrast bolus is critical for detecting aortic dissection—what phase is optimal? — Arterial phase (15‑30 s) provides clear lumen definition; late scanning may miss intimal flap.

A pregnant woman presents with suspected pulmonary embolism—what imaging strategy is safest? — Prefer ventilation‑perfusion scan; if unavailable, use lower‑dose CTPA with shielding, balancing maternal risk.

What are the key contraindications to CTA and how do you mitigate them? — Contrast allergy, severe renal impairment, pregnancy; pre‑medicate for allergy, hydrate or use alternative imaging for renal issues.
ai.title: CT Angiography
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: CT angiography (CTA) uses contrast‑enhanced CT to visualise arterial and venous anatomy quickly. It is essential for diagnosing vascular emergencies, planning interventions, and evaluating chronic disease, especially where conventional angiography is unavailable.

sections.p: CTA acquires thin‑slice CT images after intravenous iodinated contrast, reconstructed into 3‑D maps of vessels. It provides rapid, non‑invasive assessment of luminal patency, aneurysm size, and dissection.

t.b: What is the vascular anatomy and pathology? — Shows vessel lumen, stenosis, occlusion, aneurysm, dissection; guides urgent management.
Is there acute hemorrhage before contrast? — Detects bleed that would contraindicate contrast; if unavailable, assess clinically and consider MRI if possible.

b: Arterial phase: 15‑30 s after injection, best for stenosis/dissection
Venous phase: 60‑70 s, best for venous thrombosis
Beam‑hardening from metal can obscure vessels
sections.p: Understanding CTA requires knowledge of contrast dynamics, timing (arterial vs venous phase), and artefacts that can mimic disease.

t.b: When should the scan be triggered? — Ensures optimal arterial opacification; if unavailable, use fixed delay based on site (e.g., 20 s for aorta).
Is contrast safe? — eGFR < 30 mL/min/1.73 m² increases risk of contrast‑induced nephropathy; consider hydration or alternative imaging.

sections.p: CTA is first‑line for many acute vascular conditions in low‑resource settings because it is faster and more widely available than catheter angiography.

t.b: Does the patient have a dissection? — Detects intimal flap, true/false lumen; if unavailable, use bedside ultrasound for pericardial effusion and clinical scores.
Is there a pulmonary embolus? — Shows intraluminal filling defects; if contrast contraindicated, use ventilation‑perfusion scan or bedside echocardiography.

b: Identify the correct contrast phase for the suspected pathology
Link CTA findings to next therapeutic step (e.g., endovascular stent, anticoagulation)
sections.p: Examiners test integration of history, imaging choice, interpretation, and immediate management.

t.a: CTA shows a 6 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm with mural thrombus
t.b: What is the management plan? — Elective repair if symptomatic or >5.5 cm; urgent repair if ruptured or expanding >0.5 cm/6 mo.

t.a: CTA reveals a carotid artery dissection
t.b: First treatment? — Antithrombotic therapy (anticoagulation or antiplatelet) unless contraindicated; consider endovascular stenting if progressive neurologic deficit.

b: Scanning too late → venous phase, missing arterial stenosis
Confusing atherosclerotic plaque with dissection flap
sections.p: Pitfalls often arise from timing errors, misreading artefacts, and overlooking contraindications.

t.b: What does it mimic? — May look like stenosis; adjust window settings or use alternative imaging.
What does it indicate? — Active bleeding; requires urgent surgical or endovascular control.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe chest or back pain with hypotension (possible aortic rupture)
Acute neurological deficit with CTA showing large vessel occlusion (stroke)
Rapidly expanding aneurysm on serial CTA
